theme: Doctrinal Pause: The Image of God
summary: What it means to be human, image-bearing, dignity, dominion, relational, embodied
readingInstruction: Read Genesis 1:26-28, Genesis 9:6, and James 3:9 prayerfully. These three passages are short, but they are the foundation of everything the Bible says about being human. Read them aloud if you can. Notice how each one applies the doctrine of the image of God to a different situation.
settingTheScene:
Two days ago you read Genesis 1, where God made humanity in his image. Yesterday’s doctrinal day set the foundation of Scripture itself. Today we take the central claim of Genesis 1, that humanity is the image of God, and explore what it actually means. This is the most important question any human being can ask: what am I, and why does my existence matter? The Christian answer is not that humans are slightly evolved animals, or accidentally meaningful collections of atoms, or self-defining beings free to invent their own purpose. The Christian answer is that every human being bears the image of God, and that this image carries with it dignity, vocation, and destiny.

The three short passages you read today show this doctrine applied in three different ways: as the source of human dignity at creation, as the basis for the sanctity of life after the flood, and as the reason ordinary speech matters in everyday Christian behavior. The doctrine is not abstract; it presses on every part of human existence.
observation: Genesis 1:26 uses a plural, “Let us make man in our image”, which Christians have long seen as a hint of the triune nature of God.
The image of God is given to humanity as male and female together, not to one sex alone. Both fully bear the image.
The image is connected immediately to a commission: “be fruitful and multiply… have dominion.” Image-bearing is not just a status; it is a vocation.
Genesis 9:6 grounds the prohibition against murder in the image of God. To take a human life is to assault the One whose image that life bears.
James 3:9 applies the image of God to speech, cursing other people is incompatible with worshiping God, because those people bear God’s image.
Across all three passages, the image of God is never said to be partial or lost. Even fallen humans, even violent humans, even people we are tempted to curse, still bear it.
doctrinalFocus:
The doctrine of the image of God, what theologians call the imago Dei, is one of Christianity’s most distinctive contributions to human thought. Every Christian doctrine about humanity begins here. To answer the question “what is a human being?” Christians answer: a creature made in the image of God.

But what does that mean? Theologians have offered three main approaches that emphasize different aspects of the biblical witness.

The first is the substantive view, which says the image consists in some quality humans share with God, rationality, moral capacity, self-awareness, a soul, the ability to know God. There is something to this. Humans are unlike other creatures in their capacity for abstract thought, moral reflection, language, and worship.

The second is the relational view, which emphasizes that humans were made for relationship, with God, with one another, with creation itself. We image God not just in what we are, but in how we relate. The fact that Genesis 1 says we were made “male and female” right alongside the image language supports this. The Trinity itself is eternal relationship, and image-bearers are made for relationship too.

The third is the functional view, which highlights the immediate commission given in Genesis 1: dominion over creation. In the ancient Near East, kings were sometimes called the “image” of their gods, meaning the king represented the god’s rule on earth. Humanity, plural and equal, is given that role. We are not gods, but we are God’s image-bearers, his representatives in the world he made.

The fullest understanding includes all three. We image God in our being (rationality, morality, capacity for worship), in our relating (to God, to one another), and in our doing (representing his rule in creation). The image is not one thing; it is the whole shape of what it means to be human.

A critical implication: the image of God was damaged but not destroyed by the Fall. Genesis 9, written after the Fall, still grounds the value of human life in the image of God. James, written to Christians, still calls fellow humans image-bearers. Sin distorts the image; it does not erase it. Every human being you will ever meet, your closest friend, your worst enemy, the unborn child, the elderly grandmother with dementia, the criminal, the saint, the stranger you will never know, bears the image of God. This is the ground of universal human dignity.

But there is more. The New Testament reveals that the image of God is most fully expressed not in fallen Adam, but in Christ. Paul calls Jesus “the image of the invisible God” (Colossians 1:15). Christ is what we were meant to be, the true human, the second Adam. And through union with Christ, believers are being “transformed into the same image from one degree of glory to another” (2 Corinthians 3:18). Sanctification is the restoration of the image. Heaven is the image fully restored.

So when you ask “what am I?” the Christian answer comes in three tenses. You were made in God’s image. That image was marred in the Fall. And in Christ, that image is being restored, and one day will be perfectly fulfilled in glory.
interpretation:
The three passages you read show the doctrine of the image of God doing actual work in Scripture. None of them stops at “humans are special.” Each one draws an ethical conclusion from the doctrine.

Genesis 1:26-28 sets the foundation. Notice the structure: God deliberates (“Let us make”), God acts (“So God created”), and God commissions (“Be fruitful… have dominion”). Image-bearing is not a passive identity; it is a calling. To be made in God’s image is to be tasked with reflecting God’s rule in the world. Marriage, family, work, creativity, stewardship of the earth, all of these flow from this opening commission. When you raise children, build something, grow a garden, organize a project, or care for a place, you are doing image-bearing work.

Genesis 9:6 takes the doctrine into the most extreme ethical territory: the taking of human life. Right after the flood, as humanity begins again, God establishes the boundary that protects human life: “Whoever sheds the blood of man, by man shall his blood be shed, for God made man in his own image.” The reason given is theological, not pragmatic. Murder is not just a social problem or a personal tragedy. It is an attack on the image of God himself. This is why every human life, regardless of usefulness, age, ability, or status, carries an irreducible weight. To diminish a human being is to insult the One whose image that human bears.

James 3:9 brings the doctrine right into ordinary life: how you talk. “With it we bless our Lord and Father, and with it we curse people who are made in the likeness of God.” James sees a contradiction, and notice what he calls the contradiction. Not that we are inconsistent in our speech, or hypocritical, though those things are true. The contradiction is that the same God we praise has made the people we curse in his own likeness. You cannot worship God on Sunday and despise your spouse, coworker, neighbor, or political opponent on Monday. They bear the image of the One you claim to worship. Image-bearing makes every encounter with a human being an encounter with the dignity of God himself.

This is why Christianity has, throughout history, been the source of the strongest claims about universal human dignity. Not because Christians have always lived consistently, they haven’t, but because the doctrine forces the issue. If every human bears the image of God, then slavery is wrong, infanticide is wrong, racism is wrong, abuse is wrong, neglect of the poor is wrong. Not wrong because we feel they are, but wrong because God has put his image in every person, and you cannot trample on that image without trampling on God himself.

The doctrine also means something about you. You are not nothing. You are not a mistake. You are not less than anyone. The God who made the stars made you in his image, called you good, and gave you a calling to image him in the world. Whatever lies you have believed about your worth, whether from yourself or from others, Genesis 1 outranks all of them.
connection: In Genesis 1 the image of God was given. In Genesis 3 (which you read yesterday) that image was marred, humans began to image themselves as gods rather than to image the true God. But the image was not lost. Every page that follows in the Bible assumes humans still bear it: that is why Cain’s murder of Abel matters in Genesis 4, why the law protects the dignity of every Israelite, why the prophets thunder against the abuse of the poor. And the whole story climaxes in Christ, the perfect image of God in human form. Through union with him, the image in us is being restored. The doctrine of the image of God runs from Genesis 1 to the new creation, where image-bearers will reign with Christ over the renewed earth, finally being what we were always meant to be.
application:
Treat people as image-bearers. That is the daily, practical heart of this doctrine. The cashier at the store, the driver who cut you off, your spouse on a hard day, the colleague you disagree with, the family member who has hurt you, the stranger on the corner asking for change, each of them bears the image of the same God you worship. You cannot honor God while dishonoring his image.

This works two directions. It calls you to higher respect for others than the world’s standards of usefulness or attractiveness or moral worth would suggest. And it calls you to higher respect for yourself than your own self-loathing might allow. You are an image-bearer. So are they. The doctrine permits neither contempt of others nor self-contempt.

Today, identify one person in your life who is hard for you to honor. It might be someone who has wronged you, someone you find irritating, someone you have written off, or someone you simply do not notice. Think of that person as one who bears the image of God. Pray for them. Speak kindly of them, or at least refuse to speak cruelly. And ask the Spirit to keep forming Christ, the true image of God, in you, so that one day your imaging of God will be as true and as full as his.
prayerPrompts: Thank God that you were made in his image, and tell him where you struggle to believe it about yourself.
Ask him to show you someone you have treated as less than an image bearer, and to change how you see them.
Praise Jesus as the perfect image of the Father.
